# Part A

```{r}
SafeCore <- read_rds("data/SafeCore.rds")
# Factor Scores per constituent: lower values mean a lower score to the factor.
# E.g. Value of -2 means an expensive stock.
Factor_Scores <- read_rds("data/Factor_Scores.rds")
Idx_Daily <- read_rds("data/Index_Returns_Daily.rds")
# Stock returns
Stock_returns_daily <- read_rds("./data/Stock_Returns_Daily.rds")
```

## PART B
###  Did SafeCore navigate volatility well? 
Compare the fund’s volatility, beta, maximum drawdown, and up and down capture against the Capped SWIX, in calm versus stressed periods. Since volatility isn’t a design input, any result is incidental, so say that plainly.  
```{r}
# Benchmark (J433) daily returns - check the ticker label in your index file:
Bench_returns <-
    Idx_Daily
    filter(Tickers == "J433TR Index") %>%
    arrange(date) %>%
    mutate(Mkt = Price / lag(Price) - 1) %>%
    filter(!is.na(Mkt)) %>%
    select(date, Mkt)
```


### Where does the volatility come from?
Use the stock and sector risk contributions (section 7c), the PC1 share and the ENB. If ENB falls in stressed periods, the diversification is weakest when it is needed most.

### What are the factor exposures? 
Show the active low-vol and momentum scores and the regression betas. If the fund is below benchmark on low-vol, that explains higher volatility. Agreement between your scores and the third party’s strengthens the finding.

### Efficient diversifiers: I read these as stocks whose risk contribution is smaller than their weight. A stock’s risk contribution divided by its weight equals its beta to the portfolio, so a ratio below 1 means it reduces concentration. Section 7b ranks the stocks on this. Tell me if your brief means something different by “efficient”.


## Part C

Motivating Weighted vs. Unweighted CSV (J433 Capped SWIX):   Explain that Capped SWIX caps individual constituents at 10% to mitigate single-stock concentration (like Naspers/Prosus), yet large-caps still dominate institutional liquidity.Weighted CSV measures the actual investable dispersion available to an institutional fund benchmarked against J433, avoiding distortion from illiquid small-caps. Showing Equal-Weighted CSV alongside it reveals whether alpha is concentrated in mid/small caps or broad across the top 40.  

Why SAVIUSD, MOVE, and V2X Are Perfect for Your Macro Analysis:   Macro Panic Regime (e.g., March 2020 COVID shock): V2X and SAVIUSD spike violently. Notice how rolling pairwise correlations (cor_median) and PCA Absorption (pca_pc1_abs) surge toward highs—stocks move in lockstep ("correlations go to 1 in a crisis"). Even though raw CSV spikes briefly due to extreme volatility, correlation-adjusted alpha opportunity collapses because stock selection fails when macro panic drives everything.   Rate & FX Divergence Regime (2022–2023 Hiking Cycle & Local Shocks): When MOVE (US Treasury rate volatility) and SAVIUSD (Rand volatility) stay elevated without a total liquidity freeze, correlations fall back down while Weighted CSV and Beta Dispersion stay elevated. Why? Because Rand weakness (SAVIUSD) splits the JSE into two opposing camps: Rand-hedges (miners, dual-listed industrials) surging while SA Inc. (banks, retailers, property) sell off—creating peak alpha opportunity for active managers.
